title: SpiNNaker
intro: SpiNNaker (Spiking Neural Network Architecture) is a massively parallel computer built at the University of Manchester by Steve Furber's group. It does not hard-wire neurons into silicon. It uses a very large number of small, general-purpose ARM processors and a custom network designed for one job: delivering huge numbers of tiny spike packets in real time. That makes it the most flexible of the big neuromorphic platforms, since any neuron model or learning rule you can write in C runs on it.

items: The chip: each SpiNNaker chip has 18 ARM968 cores (one monitor core, up to 16 cores running neurons, one spare), local SRAM per core, 128 MB of shared SDRAM, and a multicast router.

Packets: spikes travel as small packets (40 bits, with a 32-bit routing key) using address-event representation: the packet names the neuron that fired, and the router looks up where that key should go.

Multicast routing: a single spike is replicated by routers along the way to reach all targets, which is how SpiNNaker matches biology's large fan-out (thousands of targets per neuron) without sending thousands of separate messages.

Real-time operation: each core updates its neurons every simulated millisecond, typically a few hundred neurons with their synapses per core, and processes incoming spikes as events in between. Synaptic weights live in SDRAM and are fetched when a spike arrives.

Scale: the full machine in Manchester, completed in 2018, has about one million ARM cores (57,600 chips). It was designed to simulate up to roughly a billion simple neurons in real time, around 1% of a human brain.

blocks.text: Models are written in PyNN, a simulator-independent Python API. The sPyNNaker software maps populations and projections onto cores and builds the routing tables. Plasticity, including STDP variants and structural plasticity, runs on the cores as ordinary code, so new rules mean new C code rather than new silicon.

items: Cortical microcircuit in real time. The Potjans-Diesmann model of a 1 mm² patch of early sensory cortex (about 77,000 neurons and 300 million synapses across layers 2/3, 4, 5 and 6) was first matched to NEST's accuracy on SpiNNaker by van Albada et al. (2018), and later run in biological real time (Rhodes et al. 2020). It is the closest existing benchmark to a full cortical column simulation.
Basal ganglia, cerebellum and robotics models running in closed loop with sensors and motors, thanks to real-time operation.
Part of the EU Human Brain Project's neuromorphic platform, alongside BrainScaleS.

blocks.text: The second generation, developed with TU Dresden, has 152 ARM Cortex-M4F cores per chip in a 22 nm FDSOI process, with dynamic voltage and frequency scaling per core and accelerators for exponentials, random numbers and small matrix operations. That lets it run both spiking networks and conventional deep-learning kernels, and hybrids of the two.

items: Flexibility: any model or rule, written as software.
Less energy-efficient per synaptic event than custom chips such as TrueNorth or Loihi, since general-purpose cores do the work.
Real-time operation fixes the time step (usually 1 ms) and limits how many neurons and synapses each core can handle.

blocks.text: For a cortical column: SpiNNaker is the platform on which a full-scale, multi-layer cortical microcircuit has actually run in real time. If you build your column in PyNN (or port it to PyNN once it works in JavaScript or Brian2), you can run the same model on a laptop simulator and on SpiNNaker, and compare it directly to the published Potjans-Diesmann results.
